title: Properties and reactivity
note: Alcohols and alkyl halides are classed by carbons on the carbon bearing the group; amines by carbons on N. An O–H or N–H donates hydrogen bonds; O or N lone pairs accept them. Acidity: acid > phenol > alcohol > terminal alkyne. Acyl reactivity: chloride > anhydride > thioester > ester > amide.

read.title: Degree, hydrogen bonds and carbonyl reactivity
text: Degree counts neighbors, but the counting differs by group. For an alcohol or alkyl halide, count the carbons attached to the carbon that bears the OH or halogen: one is primary, two secondary, three tertiary. For an amine, count the carbons attached to nitrogen itself. That is why tert-butylamine, (CH₃)₃C–NH₂, is a primary amine.

Hydrogen bonding follows the atoms. A molecule needs an O–H or N–H to donate, and a lone pair on O or N to accept. Ethanol does both. Diethyl ether and a tertiary amine can only accept, so they boil far lower than alcohols of similar mass.

Acidity depends on how well the conjugate base copes with its negative charge. A carboxylate spreads charge over two oxygens, so carboxylic acids (pKa about 4–5) beat phenols (about 10), which beat alcohols (about 16). Amines hold a lone pair on N and act as weak bases. Amides do not: that lone pair is tied up by the neighboring carbonyl.

Carbonyl derivatives differ in reactivity. The better the leaving group and the less the substituent donates electrons to C=O, the faster the attack: acyl chloride, anhydride, thioester, ester, amide. Reactive ones convert into less reactive ones, not directly the reverse.

q.q: Why do amides fail to act as appreciable bases?
o: The N lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl
